standing_assumptions:
Setting, notation and standing assumptions, as printed. Every passage was read from the rendered page images. Article pages are those of Political Analysis 31 (2023), with the PDF page in parentheses; the supplement is the publisher's Supporting Information (publisher-supplement.pdf, 5 pp., printed and PDF page numbers coincide).
[Notation: Section 2, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “Before we proceed, we introduce some notation. Let $n$ be the number of observations. Let $k$ be the number of variables (columns) in the dataset. Let $M_{ij}$ be a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th variable in the $i$th row is missing. For notational convenience, we will let $\mathbf{M}_{ij}$ represent the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$ $(M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$.”
[Assumption 1, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “All rows of the data $((M_{11}, \ldots, M_{1k}), \ldots, (M_{n1}, \ldots, M_{nk}))$ are mutually independent.”
[Assumption 2, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “There exists a $q_* \in [0,1)$ such that for all $i$, • $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) \leq q_*$ and • $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0) \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{2, \ldots, k\}$ such that $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0) > 0$.”
[The quantity $p_{all}$: Section 2.1, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “We begin by application of elementary probability theory to yield the following finite-$n$ result. In words, this result establishes an exact lower bound on the probability that all rows of the data will suffer from some missingness. In such instances, listwise deletion would yield no usable data.” Lemma 3 then names $p_{all}$ as “the probability that listwise deletion removes all rows”.
[The sequence: pp. 150-151 (PDF pp. 2-3)] “We can now consider the asymptotic properties of listwise deletion, letting both $k$ and $n$ tend to infinity. To do so, we embed the above problem into a sequence. We let $k_n = f(n)$, where $f$ has range over the natural numbers, and allow $M_{ij,n}$ and therefore $q_{ij,n}$ to vary at each $n$. To ease exposition, we omit notational dependence on $n$.”
[Assumption 4, p. 151 (PDF p. 3)] “The number of covariates grows superlogarithmically in $n$, so that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{f(n)}{log(n)} = \infty$.” The next sentence: “Assumption 4 can be equivalently written in asymptotic shorthand notation as $k = \omega(\log n)$.”
[Reading fixed by the printed text and used in every target] $M_{ij} = 1$ means that entry $(i,j)$ is missing and $M_{ij} = 0$ that it is observed (the proof of Lemma 3, p. 154, treats $1 - \Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ik} = 0)$ as “the probability of a single observation containing at least one missing entry”). The event written $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = 0$ is $\{M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0\}$. Row $i$ is removed by listwise deletion when at least one of $M_{i1}, \ldots, M_{ik}$ equals 1, and $p_{all}$ is the probability that every one of the $n$ rows has at least one $j$ with $M_{ij} = 1$. $q_*$ is an upper bound on a probability of being observed. It is one constant, the same for every row and, along the sequence, for every $n$; the laws of the $M_{ij,n}$ may change with $n$ (this is the reading the validator fixed for P007-N002, which was not confirmed as an error). $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 1$ are integers; $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The symbol $q_{ij}$ is defined only inside the proof of Lemma 3 (p. 154).
[Supplement, Supporting Information A, p. 1] “Here we demonstrate the finite-$n$ implications of our findings. In the following figures, we plot figures for different values of an upper bound on the conditional probability of each data entry being observed $q_*$, the number of observations (rows) $n$, the number of variables (columns) $k$ and a sharp lower bound on $p_{all}$ denoted $\underline{p_{all}} = (1 - q_*^{f(n)})^n$. $\underline{p_{all}}$ is the lowest possible (”best-case”) probability that listwise deletion removes all data.” And, same page: “By Lemma 3, we can compute $\underline{p_{all}} = (1 - q_*^k)^n$.”
[Supplement, Supporting Information B, p. 3] “Let $n$ be the number of observations. Let $g$ be the number of variable groups in the dataset, within which all observations share an identical missingness pattern. We let $M_{ij}$ be a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th group in the $i$th row is missing. We use one indicator for each group due to the shared missingness. Similar to the previous setting, we use $\mathbf{M}_{ij}$ to represent the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$, $(M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$. Let $k$ be the number of variables in the dataset. Note that, by construction, we know that $k \geq g$ since groups contain at least one variable.” [p. 4] Assumption 6: “All rows of the data $\left((M_{11}, ..., M_{1g}), ..., (M_{n1}, ..., M_{ng})\right)$ are mutually independent.” Assumption 7: “There exists a $q_* \in [0,1)$ such that for all $i$, • $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) \leq q_*$ • $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = \mathbf{0}) \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{2, \ldots, g\}$ such that $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = \mathbf{0}) > 0$”. The sequence: “Similarly, we will embed the problem into a sequence $g_n = l(n)$, where $l$ has range over the natural numbers, and allow $M_{ij,n}$ and $q_{ij,n}$ to vary at each $n$. We omit the $n$ notation for simplicity.” Assumption 9: “The number of groups of covariates grows superlogarithmically in $n$, so that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{l(n)}{log(n)} = \infty$.”
[Application: Section 3, pp. 151-152 (PDF pp. 3-4)] “We applied mild preprocessing to these datasets: we removed country code variables, and in the case of the State Failure data, to apply the principle of charity, we removed 19 variables that exhibited 100% missingness.” [Section 3.1, p. 152 (PDF p. 4)] “To do so, we conducted 25,000 simulations in each of which we drew $k$ of the variables from each dataset (without replacement). We then recorded the number of rows of the data that survive listwise deletion. We then report the expected proportion of remaining data observed after listwise deletion, as well as the probability that all rows of the data exhibit some missingness. Note that, here, expected values and probabilities refer to the randomness induced by our random subsampling procedure, not any fundamental stochasticity giving rise to the underlying data.” So in the application the data are a fixed array of missing and observed cells, and the only randomness is the uniform draw of $k$ of its variables without replacement. Assumptions 1 and 2 play no part in the targets about the application (P007-T1, P007-T2, P007-T12, P007-T13).
Scope of the targets. Headline claims that are mathematical statements: P007-H1 (Lemma 3: P007-T14), P007-H2 (Proposition 5: P007-T16) and P007-H6 (Lemma 8 and Proposition 10: P007-T15 and P007-T17). P007-H3 (the finite-$n$ illustration of the bound), P007-H4 and P007-H5 (the two data illustrations) and P007-H7 (the conclusion) are numerical illustrations, simulation results or interpretive remarks, so they are not headline targets; the formal content of the findings that touch P007-H3 and P007-H5 is in the targets below. Confirmed errors with mathematical content, each with a corrected-statement target: P007-E010 (Moderate; Table 1's State Failure average and the threshold “more than three variables”: exact refutation P007-T1, correction P007-T2, statement as printed P007-T13); P007-E003 (Minor; the printed proofs of Lemmas 3 and 8 and of Propositions 5 and 10: P007-T3 to P007-T6); P007-E005 (Minor; the Figure 4 paragraph of the supplement: P007-T7, P007-T8); P007-E006 (Minor; “upper bound” and the caption of Figure 5: P007-T9, P007-T10); P007-E004 (Minor; “i.i.d.” for Assumption 1: P007-T11); P007-E014 (Minor; its established part is the same stale Table 1 average: P007-T12). Confirmed errors that are not targets, because their corrections change no mathematical statement: P007-E009 (Moderate; the analysed file is the QoG Basic dataset and not the Standard dataset that is cited, a matter of data provenance, and every QoG number stands for the deposited file); P007-E001 (the glmnet software example); P007-E013 (a garbled reference entry); within P007-E004, the misprint “out” for “our”; within P007-E014, the behaviour of the is.na mask on empty Stata strings (a property of the code whose effect on the State Failure data was not established). Not targets because they are not rated as errors: P007-E002 and P007-N001 (clarity notes), P007-N002, P007-N004, P007-N005 and P007-N006 (not confirmed), P007-N003 (undetermined), P007-N007 (out of scope).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.1, third paragraph: the two descriptions of Assumption 1 as “i.i.d. missingness across rows”, as repaired by Sol
canonical_claim.location: p. 152 (PDF p. 4), Section 3.1, third paragraph, second and last sentences; Assumption 1 is on p. 150 (PDF p. 2)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 152 (PDF p. 4)] “We briefly discuss how out theoretical assumptions align with this setting. Assumption 1 asserts i.i.d. missingness across rows, which is unlikely to be met in this setting.” And, at the end of the paragraph: “Our theoretical assumption of i.i.d. missingness across rows can therefore be seen as optimistic when faced with real-world data and, all else equal, the probability that all data will be lost may be higher than theory might dictate.” [Printed, Assumption 1, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “All rows of the data $((M_{11}, \ldots, M_{1k}), \ldots, (M_{n1}, \ldots, M_{nk}))$ are mutually independent.”
[Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P007-E004), verbatim] “Replace out theoretical assumptions by our theoretical assumptions; replace both occurrences of i.i.d. missingness across rows by mutually independent missingness across rows.” [The two sentences as corrected] “Assumption 1 asserts mutually independent missingness across rows, which is unlikely to be met in this setting.” “Our theoretical assumption of mutually independent missingness across rows can therefore be seen as optimistic when faced with real-world data and, all else equal, the probability that all data will be lost may be higher than theory might dictate.”
[Mathematical content]
(i) Assumption 1 is the mutual independence of the $n$ row vectors $(M_{i1}, \ldots, M_{ik})$. Neither it nor Assumption 2 requires the rows to have the same distribution.
(ii) [The validator's witness that the assumptions do not entail identical distribution.] Let $n = 2$ and $k = 1$, with $M_{11}$ and $M_{21}$ independent, $\Pr(M_{11} = 0) = \frac{1}{4}$ and $\Pr(M_{21} = 0) = \frac{1}{2}$. Then Assumption 1 holds; Assumption 2 holds with $q_* = \frac{1}{2}$ ($\frac{1}{4} \leq \frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{1}{2}$); the two rows are not identically distributed ($\frac{1}{4} \neq \frac{1}{2}$); and the conclusion of Lemma 3 holds: $p_{all} = \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{8} \geq \left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}$.
(iii) [What the proof of Lemma 3 uses.] Under Assumption 1 alone, with $s_{ik} = \Pr(M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ik} = 0)$ the probability that row $i$ is complete, $p_{all} = \prod_{i=1}^{n}(1 - s_{ik})$, a product of row-specific factors; no common value of the $s_{ik}$ is needed for Lemma 3 (P007-T5 (e)).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] $n$, the number of observations; $k$, the number of variables (columns); $M_{ij}$, “a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th variable in the $i$th row is missing”; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = (M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$, “the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$”; Assumption 1 and Assumption 2 as transcribed in standing_assumptions; $p_{all}$, “the probability that listwise deletion removes all rows” (Lemma 3, p. 150). Reading: $M_{ij} = 1$ missing, $M_{ij} = 0$ observed; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = 0$ is the event $\{M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0\}$; $p_{all} = \Pr(\text{every row } i \text{ has some } j \text{ with } M_{ij} = 1)$. “i.i.d.” is not defined in the paper; it is read in its standard sense, independent and identically distributed rows.
canonical_claim.note: The most marginal target on the list: a label for an assumption whose formal statement is unambiguous. It is included because P007-E004 is rated an error (Minor), the label adds a condition (identical distribution) to a mathematical assumption, and the author's instruction covers every confirmed error in a mathematical statement at any severity. The rater notes that the label on its own would be a clarity note; the misprint “out” for “our” in the same paragraph is a spelling slip and is not a target. Part (ii) is the batch validator's exact example (derivations.md, section E004, and checks-output.json in the same folder: row observed probabilities 1/4 and 1/2, p_all 3/8, lemma lower bound 1/4). Part (iii) restates P007-T5 (e) and adds nothing to prove beyond it. Nothing depends on the label: the paragraph's discussion (clustering of countries and of country-years) concerns independence only, and no result uses identical distribution.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Table 1, State Failure column, “Proportion of missing values (avg.)”, corrected for the 1,205 retained variables (the part of P007-E014 that is established)
canonical_claim.location: Table 1, p. 152 (PDF p. 4); preprocessing sentence, pp. 151-152 (PDF pp. 3-4); replication script Simcode_Statefailure.R, lines 28-55
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, Table 1, p. 152 (PDF p. 4), State Failure column] Number of observations: 8,580. Number of variables: 1,205. Proportion of missing values (avg.): 66.8%. [Printed, pp. 151-152] “We applied mild preprocessing to these datasets: we removed country code variables, and in the case of the State Failure data, to apply the principle of charity, we removed 19 variables that exhibited 100% missingness.”
[Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P007-E014, prior_correction.corrected_text), first sentence, verbatim] “Recompute the State Failure average after removing the 19 wholly missing columns; under the original is.na mask, the saved log implies a retained average of 66.3%.” [Sol's smallest repair, first sentence] “Change the State Failure average in Table 1 to 66.3% and recompute prop.missing <- mean(colMeans(isnamatrix)) immediately after the retained-mask assignment at line 44.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis]
[Setting] Integers $n \geq 1$, $K \geq 1$ and $d \geq 0$, with $R = K + d$; an array $m \in \{0,1\}^{n \times R}$ ($m_{ij} = 1$: cell missing) in which $d$ of the $R$ columns are entirely missing ($m_{ij} = 1$ for all $i$). $q_{before} = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{j=1}^{R}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{ij}\right)$ is the average over all $R$ columns of the column missing proportions, and $q_{after}$ is the same average over the $K$ columns that remain when those $d$ columns are removed. $A = \sum_{i,j} m_{ij}$ is the number of missing cells before removal.
(i) [Identity] $q_{before} = \dfrac{A}{nR}$, $q_{after} = \dfrac{A - nd}{nK}$, and $R\,q_{before} = d + K\,q_{after}$; that is, $q_{after} = \dfrac{R\,q_{before} - d}{K}$.
(ii) [The printed average cannot describe the retained variables.] With $n = 8580$, $K = 1205$, $d = 19$ and $R = 1224$: if $q_{before}$ is 66.8% to one decimal place, that is $0.6675 \leq q_{before} < 0.6685$, then $q_{after} < \dfrac{1224 \cdot 0.6685 - 19}{1205} = \dfrac{199811}{301250} < 0.6675$, so $q_{after}$ is not 66.8% to one decimal place.
(iii) [The corrected entry and the size of the overstatement.] With the count implied by the authors' log, $A = 7019387$ (P007-T2 (i)): $q_{before} = \dfrac{7019387}{10501920}$; $q_{after} = \dfrac{6856367}{10338900}$, which satisfies $0.6625 \leq q_{after} < 0.6635$ (66.3%); and $q_{before} - q_{after} = \dfrac{66168127}{12654813600}$, that is, the printed entry overstates the average for the retained variables by $\dfrac{66168127}{126548136} \approx 0.5229$ percentage points.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Table 1, p. 152] “Proportion of missing values (avg.)”: the average over variables of the proportion of rows in which the variable is missing, as computed by the script (mean(colMeans(isnamatrix))); “missing” is the script's is.na mask. [pp. 151-152] the 19 removed variables “exhibited 100% missingness”. [Script and log] Simcode_Statefailure.R assigns prop.missing once, at line 29, before the columns of maximum missingness are removed at lines 39-40, and prints it at line 55 beside the retained dimensions; the log prints 8580, 1205 and 0.668390827582004.
canonical_claim.note: P007-E014 is confirmed in part and rated Minor. What is established is this stale average, which is the same defect as the first part of P007-E010 (P007-T2 (i)); the statement here is the adjudicator's complete derivation (section “Finite-sum identity and a proof that the printed average is wrong”), whose part (ii) needs only the printed dimensions and the count of removed columns, together with the fact that the printed figure is the pre-removal average. That fact is a property of the script and is not a Lean matter. Parts (i) and (ii) hold for every array meeting the stated preprocessing, whatever the arrangement of its missing cells; part (iii) uses the count inferred from the log, not a recount of the data. The rest of P007-E014 is not a target: that the is.na mask counts empty Stata strings as observed is a property of the code, shown on synthetic data only; whether the State Failure data contain such blanks, and every number proposed for a blank-aware mask, were not established. All fractions were recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.location: p. 150 (PDF p. 2), Section 2.1; proof in the Appendix, p. 154 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] Lemma 3. Under Assumptions 1 and 2, the probability that listwise deletion removes all rows is $p_{all} \geq (1 - q_*^k)^n$.
[Hypotheses, p. 150] Assumption 1. All rows of the data $((M_{11}, \ldots, M_{1k}), \ldots, (M_{n1}, \ldots, M_{nk}))$ are mutually independent. Assumption 2. There exists a $q_* \in [0,1)$ such that for all $i$, • $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) \leq q_*$ and • $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0) \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{2, \ldots, k\}$ such that $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0) > 0$.
[Text introducing the lemma, p. 150] “We begin by application of elementary probability theory to yield the following finite-$n$ result. In words, this result establishes an exact lower bound on the probability that all rows of the data will suffer from some missingness. In such instances, listwise deletion would yield no usable data.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] $n$, the number of observations; $k$, the number of variables (columns); $M_{ij}$, “a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th variable in the $i$th row is missing”; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = (M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$, “the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$”; Assumption 1 and Assumption 2 as transcribed in standing_assumptions; $p_{all}$, “the probability that listwise deletion removes all rows” (Lemma 3, p. 150). Reading: $M_{ij} = 1$ missing, $M_{ij} = 0$ observed; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = 0$ is the event $\{M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0\}$; $p_{all} = \Pr(\text{every row } i \text{ has some } j \text{ with } M_{ij} = 1)$. The $q_*$ of the conclusion is the $q_*$ of Assumption 2: the bound is asserted for every $q_* \in [0,1)$ for which the two conditions of Assumption 2 hold for all rows.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P007-H1; an exact finite-sample statement. Both readers re-derived it and the validator's derivation proves it as printed, including rows in which a prefix event has probability zero. The printed proof has the defects of P007-E003 (P007-T3, P007-T4); the repaired chain is P007-T5, whose part (e) is this lemma. Not part of the printed lemma, recorded for the formalizer: the bound is attained when all $n \cdot k$ indicators are independent with $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0) = q_*$ (the supplement's “sharp lower bound”; see P007-T8 (iv)); and independence across rows is needed for the product form (a reader's check: $n = 2$, $k = 1$, each row observed with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and exactly one of the two rows observed, gives $p_{all} = 0 < \frac{1}{4}$).

canonical_claim.location: Supplement p. 4 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 4), Supporting Information B; proof on the same page
canonical_claim.statement:
[Supplement p. 4] Lemma 8. Under Assumptions 6 and 7, the probability that listwise deletion removes all rows is $p_{all} \geq (1 - q_*^g)^n$.
[Hypotheses, Supplement p. 4] Assumption 6. All rows of the data $\left((M_{11}, ..., M_{1g}), ..., (M_{n1}, ..., M_{ng})\right)$ are mutually independent. Assumption 7. There exists a $q_* \in [0,1)$ such that for all $i$, • $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) \leq q_*$ • $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = \mathbf{0}) \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{2, \ldots, g\}$ such that $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = \mathbf{0}) > 0$.
[Text introducing the lemma, Supplement pp. 3-4] “We will restate Assumption 1 and 2 in the group settings in Assumption 6 and 7 such that there is mutual independence of missingness across rows as well as the conditional probability that an observation is missing being bounded away from zero.” “Then we can obtain a group version of Lemma 3 (Lemma 8) following similar steps.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Supplement p. 3] $g$, “the number of variable groups in the dataset, within which all observations share an identical missingness pattern”; $M_{ij}$, “a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th group in the $i$th row is missing”; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = (M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$ (printed “up to variable $j$”; the indicators are those of groups $1, \ldots, j$); $k$, the number of variables, with $k \geq g$. [Supplement p. 4] Assumptions 6 and 7 as transcribed in standing_assumptions. A row is complete exactly when all $g$ of its group indicators are 0, and $p_{all}$ is the probability that every row has at least one group indicator equal to 1.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P007-H6 (the extension to groups of variables that share one missingness pattern); an exact finite-sample statement. It is Lemma 3 with one indicator per group and $g$ in place of $k$, and it holds as printed; the printed proof has the same defects as that of Lemma 3 (P007-T3 (vi), P007-T4 (viii)) and the repaired chain is P007-T5 with $h = g$. A formalization may state Lemma 3 and Lemma 8 as one statement about $h$ binary indicators per row; if the variables are modelled as well, the content of the grouping is that a row is complete in all $k$ variables exactly when all $g$ group indicators are 0, and that $g \leq k$ (Supplement p. 3).

canonical_claim.location: p. 151 (PDF p. 3), Section 2.1; proof in the Appendix, p. 154 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 151 (PDF p. 3)] Proposition 5. Under Assumptions 1, 2, and 4, $\lim_{n\to\infty} p_{all} = 1$.
[Hypotheses] Assumptions 1 and 2 (p. 150), as transcribed in P007-T14. Assumption 4 (p. 151). The number of covariates grows superlogarithmically in $n$, so that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{f(n)}{log(n)} = \infty$.
[The sequence to which the limit refers, pp. 150-151] “We can now consider the asymptotic properties of listwise deletion, letting both $k$ and $n$ tend to infinity. To do so, we embed the above problem into a sequence. We let $k_n = f(n)$, where $f$ has range over the natural numbers, and allow $M_{ij,n}$ and therefore $q_{ij,n}$ to vary at each $n$. To ease exposition, we omit notational dependence on $n$.” [Sentence before the proposition, p. 151] “The following proposition demonstrates that when Assumptions 1, 2, and 4 hold, then the probability of listwise deletion yielding no usable data tends to 1 as $n \to \infty$.”
[The statement with the suppressed index restored] For each $n \geq 1$ let $k_n = f(n)$ and let $(M_{ij,n})$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, $j = 1, \ldots, k_n$, be indicators on a probability space that may depend on $n$, with $p_{all,n}$ the probability that every one of the $n$ rows has at least one $j$ with $M_{ij,n} = 1$. Suppose that for every $n$ the $n$ rows are mutually independent (Assumption 1), that there is one $q_* \in [0,1)$ for which the two conditions of Assumption 2 hold for every $n$ and every row, and that $f(n)/\log(n) \to \infty$ (Assumption 4). Then $p_{all,n} \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] $n$, the number of observations; $k$, the number of variables (columns); $M_{ij}$, “a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th variable in the $i$th row is missing”; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = (M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$, “the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$”; Assumption 1 and Assumption 2 as transcribed in standing_assumptions; $p_{all}$, “the probability that listwise deletion removes all rows” (Lemma 3, p. 150). Reading: $M_{ij} = 1$ missing, $M_{ij} = 0$ observed; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = 0$ is the event $\{M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0\}$; $p_{all} = \Pr(\text{every row } i \text{ has some } j \text{ with } M_{ij} = 1)$. [pp. 150-151] $k_n = f(n)$, “where $f$ has range over the natural numbers”; $M_{ij,n}$ and $q_{ij,n}$ vary with $n$; the index $n$ is omitted in the printed statement. $q_*$ does not depend on $n$ (see standing_assumptions). [p. 151] “Assumption 4 can be equivalently written in asymptotic shorthand notation as $k = \omega(\log n)$.”
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The printed proof (p. 154, PDF p. 6) rests on the following, for each fixed $n$: (1) Lemma 3 at each $n$ and the trivial upper bound: “$\forall n, (1 - q_*^{f(n)})^n \leq p_{all} \leq 1$” (last line of the proof; P007-T14). (2) Bernoulli's inequality: $1 - nq_*^{f(n)} \leq (1 - q_*^{f(n)})^n \leq 1$ for $f(n) \geq 1$ (third paragraph of the proof, printed with misprints; corrected in P007-T6 (a)); hence $0 \leq 1 - p_{all} \leq nq_*^{f(n)}$ (P007-T6 (b)). (3) For $q_* \in (0,1)$ and $n \geq 1$: $nq_*^{f(n)} = e^{\log nq_*^{f(n)}} = e^{\log n + f(n)\log q_*}$ and $\log q_* < 0$ (first display and the line after it). (4) The endpoint omitted from the printed proof: if $q_* = 0$ and $f(n) \geq 1$ then $p_{all} = 1$ (P007-T5 (a), P007-T6 (c)). The limit steps printed after these are: $\log n + f(n)\log q_* \to -\infty$ because $f(n) = \omega(\log n)$, so $\lim_{n\to\infty} nq_*^{f(n)} = 0$; then the squeeze theorem twice, giving $\lim_{n\to\infty}(1 - q_*^{f(n)})^n = 1$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty} p_{all} = 1$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P007-H2, the paper's main result. It holds as printed under the natural reading in which $q_*$ is one constant for the whole sequence; both readers followed the proof and the validators give a complete derivation (runs/P007/validate/P007-E003/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section “General proof of Propositions 5 and 10, including q_*=0”). The validator_artifact is the Lean file written for P007-N002 (not confirmed as an error): it proves the analytic content for one fixed $q \in [0,1)$, including $q = 0$ (uniform_decay: $n\,q^{k_n} \to 0$ when $k_n/\log n \to \infty$; proposition5_fixed_bound; proposition5_from_row_survival), for real sequences, without the probability space; the probability steps are in its derivation.md. It compiled without sorry and may be reused once checked against this statement. The reading in which each $n$ has its own bound $q_{*,n}$ is a different and weaker hypothesis under which the conclusion can fail (the candidate's example had $q_{*,n} = 1 - n^{-2}$); it is not the printed statement and is not a target. Remarks from the audit that are not part of the printed proposition: the conclusion also follows from the union bound $1 - p_{all} \leq nq_*^{f(n)}$ without Assumption 1; and the abstract's “for large $n$, listwise deletion will drop all rows with probability 1” (P007-N001, a clarity note) is loose wording for this limit. Printed misprints in the proof ($\geq_*$, an unbalanced exponent) are corrected in P007-T6.
